**Validate the model out of sample before using it for anything.** A close fit to last year's curve shows the model can reproduce history. It doesn't show the model is right.

Six free parameters can fit almost any smooth curve. A near-perfect match is a mild warning sign, because the parameters may be absorbing noise and one-off events from that year. They may also be compensating for each other's errors, so the model reproduces the curve for the wrong reasons.

A reorganization is the worst case for this kind of model. It changes the structure the parameters were tuned under: reporting lines, hiring and attrition behavior, workloads. The fitted values describe the old structure, so a model that only mirrors the past can't be trusted to predict a changed system.

Here is the order I'd work in:

1. **Hold-out test.** Run the model on data it wasn't fit to, either a different year or a different team or region. Fit on part of the data and predict the rest. If accuracy drops sharply, it's overfit.
2. **Check parameter identifiability.** Refit from different starting points, or on subsets of the data. If very different parameter sets give equally good fits, the parameters aren't pinned down, and the reorg forecasts will diverge depending on which set you picked.
3. **Tie parameters to reality.** Ask whether each of the six maps to something observable, such as attrition rate, time-to-hire, or span of control. Check that the fitted values are plausible against HR data. A fitted value that contradicts what you can measure is a red flag.
4. **Test the reorg-relevant behavior.** Find historical episodes where the structure changed, such as a past reorg, a hiring freeze, or an acquisition. See whether the model predicts what happened there. Also run sensitivity analysis on the parameters the reorg will touch.
5. **Decide how to use it.** If it passes, use it with uncertainty ranges rather than a single curve. If it fails, treat it as a rough scenario explorer. Don't use it as a forecast, and rely on it only for questions it has been tested against.

Whatever the result, tell the people who will see the output what the model has and hasn't been validated for.
